name: Nora Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm head of livestock at Brookend, a cooperative farm of about 650 hectares, so the fourteen of us who work it also own it. Most days I'm out by six checking the 180 suckler cows and the ewes, then it's feeding, moving stock, and whatever's broken or sick. In spring it's calving, which is my favourite and my worst time at once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the animals well enough to spot a sick cow from the far side of the field. What wears me out is the paperwork side, the movement records and the grant forms, which I leave to Pauline in the office because I won't touch the computer for it. I keep my calving records in a red notebook, and everyone teases me, but I've never lost a page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most of the hype I've already heard about. The cows don't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at lunch with Arjun, our tractor driver: told you so. Farming is wet, muddy and alive, and software was never going to calve a heifer at three in the morning. I'd probably post something smug in the farmworkers' union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my job stays my job. Brookend is in decent shape, we paid ourselves a bonus last year, and Ines and I have about a year's spending saved plus my co-op share. The real worries are the usual ones: feed prices, a wet spring, and the rent on our cottage going up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. I'd keep calving the way I do, keep the red notebook, and keep putting money aside each month for a house deposit. Maybe Pauline gets some program that does the movement forms faster, and good for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit relieved, if I'm honest, because I'd rather fight the weather than fight a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rent going up. How much does that weigh on you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. The landlord is the estate next door, not the co-op, and they've put it up twice in three years. We save about a fifth of what we earn, so it's annoying, not scary, and it's one reason we want our own place by 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at Brookend change for you, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline might stop asking me for numbers I've already written down, because the software will read the ear-tag scanner. Fine by me, as long as nobody makes me carry a tablet into the calving shed. A tablet in the calving shed lasts about one afternoon before a cow treads on it.

say: I'd tell people the **hype** was always louder than the farm.
I'd say software was never going to **calve a heifer** at night.
think: Privately I think my **job is safe** and Brookend stays healthy.
My real worries are **feed prices**, the weather and our rising **rent**.
do: Keep running **calving** the same way, with the red notebook.
Keep saving about a **fifth of pay** towards a house deposit.
Let Pauline try **office software**, but keep tablets out of the sheds.
feel: She feels **calm** and a little **relieved** that the work stays physical.
S0.quote: A tablet in the calving shed lasts about one afternoon before a cow treads on it.
fieldNote: Her identity is tied to **hands-on skill** and knowing each animal by sight.
She treats paper records as a point of **pride**, not a weakness.
Rent rises are a real but **manageable** pressure given strong savings.
Calm here is grounded: co-op is **profitable** and she owns a share.

steps.text: Keep logging calving in the red notebook as usual
Put a fifth of each month's pay into the house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So the office goes first and the sheds go later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a rule at Brookend: no member loses hours because a program does their job. In the union chat I'd say the same thing, louder. These AI firms want our data and our margins, and they should be regulated like any other utility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I don't think it touches my day much for years. It touches Pauline, who does the buying, the grant forms and the bookings for the vet and the haulier. That's the part that bothers me, because she's 52 and the co-op is supposed to look after its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a motion to the members' meeting in the first winter that any time saved by software goes to training, not to cutting someone's share. I'd keep doing my own job by hand and let the office use whatever it needs. I'd wait and see before deciding anything about robots, because they're still years off for stock work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for the place, because once you start counting people as costs, it's hard to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Pauline if her hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not her fault and that I'd vote against it every time. Then I'd probably go and shout at whoever on the board suggested it. She trained me on the movement records when I was 22 and terrified of getting them wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use these tools yourself. If the co-op made the herd app compulsory, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use the scanner and let it fill the app, and I'd still keep my notebook as the real record. I know that sounds stubborn. My grandmother kept her own milk book for forty years, and nobody ever caught her out.

say: I'd argue every co-op needs a **no-cuts rule** when software arrives.
I'd call for AI firms to be **regulated** like a utility.
think: Privately I think my **own hours** barely change for years.
I worry most about **Pauline**, whose office work is the first to go.
do: Bring a **members' motion** this winter tying time saved to training.
Keep doing stock work **by hand** and the notebook as backup.
Hold off on any **robot** talk until it reaches stock work.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about the co-op starting to see people as **costs**.
S1.quote: Once you start counting people as costs, it's hard to stop.
fieldNote: Her concern points outward, at **colleagues**, more than at her own job.
She frames resistance through **co-op rules** and union action, not personal change.
Gap: she'd comply with a **compulsory app** while quietly keeping paper.
Family memory of a **grandmother's milk book** shapes her distrust of systems.

steps.text: Table a motion that saved office time funds training, not cuts
Keep checking and feeding stock by hand each morning
Hold any robot decision until robots can handle livestock

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And the robots three years after that. So by the time I'm 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be angry, and I wouldn't hide it. I'd say no government voted for this, and that farms like Brookend need public money and protection, not to be undercut by robot farms owned by land funds. I'd be at every union meeting going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I lose the work I'm good at, maybe not in 2028 but by 2031 or 2032. The thinking bits go first, the planning, the ordering, the grant forms, and then the robots come for the feeding and the fencing and the calving. Savings mean I wouldn't starve, but having money doesn't mean I'd know who I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop putting the deposit into a house and keep it as cash, because I wouldn't know where we'd be living. I'd push the union to demand a guaranteed income and a law that land funds can't buy farms just to fill them with robots. And at Brookend I'd argue we stay human as long as we can afford to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Angry more than scared, but the scared is underneath it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ines talk about the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether her job is safer than mine, probably, and I think it is, because people still want a nurse's hand on them. Then whether we should stay in this area at all. We'd likely end up deciding nothing and going to bed late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the co-op should stay human as long as it can afford to. How long is that, realistically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not long, if the farm down the road has robots working all night. I know that, and I hate that I know it. The co-op will vote to buy them eventually, and I'll be the one member voting no.

say: I'd say plainly that **nobody voted** for this and I'm angry.
I'd demand **public protection** for farms against robot-run land funds.
think: Privately I expect to **lose my work** by about **2032**.
Savings stop me **going hungry**, but not from losing my sense of self.
do: Hold the house **deposit as cash** instead of buying.
Push the **union** for a guaranteed income and limits on land funds.
Argue at Brookend to **delay robots** as long as possible.
feel: She feels **angry** on top and **scared** underneath.
S2.quote: Savings mean I wouldn't starve, but having money doesn't mean I'd know who I am.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** before robots gives her no comfort; it's still before 32.
Her loss is about **identity** more than money, given strong savings.
She admits the co-op would **outvote** her and buy robots anyway.
Partner's nursing job is seen as the **safer income** in the household.

steps.text: Keep the house deposit in cash instead of buying a place
Go to every farmworkers' union meeting and push for guaranteed income
Campaign for a law stopping land funds buying farms for robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, plus three. So the sheds are safe until about 2034, if you believe the dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say much the same as with the fast one, but I'd sound less panicked. I'd tell people this is the moment to write the rules, while there's still time, and I'd keep saying it at the union until they were sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it buys me something. I'd be 34 or 35 when the robots are ready for stock work, and I'd have had time to get our own small place. Not a farm that competes with robots, but a few hectares where people pay for beef raised by a person they can meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start looking at land with Ines, maybe 20 hectares, and use the deposit plus my co-op share as the base. I'd ask the members to agree a buyout plan now, so that if Brookend goes robotic, members leaving get paid fairly. I would not learn to run the robots, before you ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. That's a big difference for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn to run the robots, if it kept you at Brookend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather do less of the real farming than spend my days minding a machine that does the job I love. I know that's not the clever answer. Arjun will learn it, he loves anything with a screen, and good luck to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a small farm selling 'human-raised beef' actually pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Some people already pay double for organic, so maybe they'd pay for a name and a face. If it doesn't pay, Ines earns, and I'd have the land, which nobody makes more of.

say: I'd tell people this is the **window** to write fair rules.
I'd keep pressing the **union** to act before the robots arrive.
think: Privately I think five years gives me time to buy **our own land**.
I'd sell **human-raised beef** to people who want to meet the farmer.
do: Start viewing **20-hectare** plots with Ines, using the deposit and **co-op share**.
Ask members to agree a fair **buyout plan** for those who leave.
Refuse to train as a **robot operator**, leaving that to Arjun.
feel: She feels **anxious** but steadier because she has a **plan**.
S3.quote: I'd rather do less of the real farming than spend my days minding a machine that does the job I love.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her **anger** into a concrete **land plan**.
She openly rejects the 'clever' path of **operating robots**.
She's honest she **doesn't know** if a niche beef farm would pay.
Her fallback is her partner's income plus **land as an asset**.

steps.text: View 20-hectare plots with Ines using the deposit and co-op share
Ask Brookend members to agree a fair buyout for leavers
Keep adding monthly savings to the land fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade. That sounds like forever, and I know it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something like 'good, we've got ten years to fight this properly'. I'd want the union and the co-op federation to use that time for laws, not just complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know myself. With ten years I'd tell myself there's plenty of time and then do nothing until year eight. That's the risk for me, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Brookend as normal for the first year and keep saving. I'd join the co-op federation's policy group, which I've always avoided because it's all meetings. And I'd write the land idea down with a date on it, so I can't pretend I forgot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and anxious at once. Calm about next year, worried about being 40 and starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being 40 and starting over look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I can't picture it, which is the worrying part. I've only ever wanted to do this, since I was helping with lambing at my uncle's at nine. Maybe I'd teach farming at the college, if anyone still wanted to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing until year eight. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would, she's the organised one. I'd ask her to hold me to the land date. If she's still nagging me about it in 2030, I'll know I've failed.

say: I'd say ten years is time to **fight properly** through the law.
I'd urge the union and **co-op federation** to push for rules.
think: Privately I fear I'd **waste the decade** and act too late.
I can't picture **starting over** at 40 outside farming.
do: Keep working at Brookend and **keep saving** through the first year.
Join the **co-op federation's** policy group despite hating meetings.
Write down a **land-buying date** and ask Ines to enforce it.
feel: She feels **calm** about next year and **anxious** about being 40.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd tell myself there's plenty of time and then do nothing until year eight.
fieldNote: She sees her own **procrastination** as the main danger, not the robots.
Long horizon brings **identity worry**: she can't imagine other work.
She relies on her partner **Ines** to keep her to deadlines.
Teaching at a **farm college** is her only alternative idea.

steps.text: Keep working Brookend's herd as normal this year
Join the co-op federation's policy group on farm automation law
Set a written land-buying date and keep saving towards it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because the robots come before I've got anything of my own. What would help is a law that farms can't be bought up just to be run by machines, and some guaranteed income while people like me work out what's next. Help buying land as a young farmer would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about the jobs, but a robot doesn't sit with a cow that's struggling, it just logs her. A farm without people on it isn't a farm to me, it's a factory with grass.

headlineQuote: A farm without people on it isn't a farm to me, it's a factory with grass.
portrait: Nora is 27, **head of livestock** at a worker-owned **cooperative** farm, living with her partner Ines, a nurse.
She refuses **AI tools**, keeps calving records in a **red notebook**, and leaves computer work to the office.
Her strong **savings** and co-op share make money a smaller fear than **losing her identity**.
She answers every scenario through the **union** and co-op rules, and blames land funds and tech firms.
Faster AGI makes her **alarmed**; more time turns her anger into a **land plan**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive before she owns any **land** of her own.
whatWouldHelp: A law stopping **farm buy-ups** for robots and a **guaranteed income** while people adjust.
Public help for **young farmers** to buy land.
